metadata.title: On The Weak Order of Orthogonal Groups

extraction_notes.note: Theorem 1.1 has no proof environment; its proof is the reduction ClP1 plus the complete-lattice claim of Section 6 and duality (Lemma 4.4). Condition (7) is never checked and the identification of the weak order with L_n is left implicit, so TP1 is marked semi_formal and linked by uses edges only.

The proof that L_n is a complete lattice is prose split around Lemmas 6.1 and 6.2; two proof nodes. PP21 ends after the 'Recall the definition...' sentence, because its own last sentence has no period; the two Definition refs there are marked as mentions.

Theorems 5.2, 5.3 and 5.4 are proved by a joint induction on n (each uses joins in L_{n-1}, i.e. Theorem 5.4 one dimension down). No edge TP8 -> PP16/PP17 was added, since it would create a results-only cycle with PP18's use of 5.2 and 5.3; the base case ClP4 is linked instead.

The proofs cite Lemma 4.6 (label boundary) as 'Theorem \ref{boundary}'; the ref resolves to the lemma. Some sign conventions in the proofs (e.g. PP6, PP17) are inconsistent with the definition of H_u, copied verbatim.

Trivial notation sentences in Section 2 (subset, element, chain, x perp y, the isometry identity for O_{n+1}, S^n = Phi^+ cup Phi^-) and the motivational remarks on functor rootoids were not made nodes.
Definition 3.9 (maximal pointed convex cone) kept origin paper, although Section 3 says it follows Fenchel's terminology; Definitions 3.1 and 3.10 are marked external (Fenchel).

nodes.name: signed group-set
nodes.statement: In \cite{Dyer} A signed group-set is defined to be a pair $(G,\Phi)$ satisfying the following conditions: \begin{enumerate}\item[(1)] $G$ is a group \item[(2)] $\Phi$ is a set with a given left action $(g,x)\mapsto gx$ by the product group $G\times \{\pm 1\}$. This action defines a pair of commuting left actions, by $G$ and $\{\pm 1\}$ on $\Phi$. \item[(3)] There is a specified partition $\Phi=\Phi^{+}\cup \Phi^{-}$ of $\Phi$ in to two disjoint subsets which are interchanged by the action of $-1$.
differentia: $\Phi$ is a set with  a given left action $(g,x)\mapsto gx$ by the product  group $G\times \{\pm 1\}$
There is a specified partition  $\Phi=\Phi^{+}\cup \Phi^{-}$ of $\Phi$ in to two disjoint subsets which are interchanged by the action of $-1$
nodes.statement_short: A signed group-set is a group G with a set Phi carrying a G x {+-1} action and a partition into positive and negative parts swapped by -1.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I

nodes.name: root system and positive roots of a signed group-set
nodes.statement: We call $\Phi$ the root system of $(G,\Phi)$ and $\Phi^{+}$ the set of positive roots.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I

nodes.name: $\Phi_g$ (positive roots made negative)
nodes.statement: For every $g\in G$, we define the subset $ \Phi_{g}:=\Phi^{+}\cap g(\Phi^{-})$. This is the set of positive roots which are made negative by $g^{-1}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I

nodes.name: weak order of a signed group-set
nodes.statement: The weak order of $(G,\Phi)$ is defined to be the set $\mathcal{L}:=\{\, \Phi_{g}\mid g\in G\,\}$ of subsets of $\Phi^{+}$, partially ordered by inclusion.
nodes.genus: set $\mathcal{L}:=\{\, \Phi_{g}\mid g\in G\,\}$ of subsets of $\Phi^{+}$
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I

nodes.name: weak order of a Coxeter system as a signed group-set
nodes.statement: For a Coxeter system $(W,S)$, the usual standard root system $\Phi$ of $(W,S)$ together with a choice $\Phi^{+}$ of positive roots give rise to a signed group-set $(W,\Phi)$. The weak-order of this signed group set is exactly the usual weak order of $W$.
nodes.statement_short: The standard root system of a Coxeter system gives a signed group-set whose weak order is the usual weak order.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I

nodes.name: rootoidal signed group-set
nodes.statement: In \cite{Dyer}, $(G,S)$ is said to be rootoidal if the following additional conditions hold: \begin{enumerate}\item[(4)] If $g\in {G}$ with $\Phi_{g}=\emptyset$ then $g=1_{G}$. \item[(5)] $\mathcal{L}$ is a complete meet semilattice i.e. each of its non-empty subsets has a meet (greatest lower boind). \item[(6)] Given a non-empty family $(A_{i})_{i\in I}$ of $\mathcal{L}$ and $B\in \mathcal{L}$ such that $A_{i}\cap B=\emptyset$ for all $i\in I$, if the join (least upper bound) $A:=\bigvee_{i\in I} A_{i}$ exists in $\mathcal{L}$, then $A\cap B=\emptyset$. (This condition is called the JTP).
differentia: $\mathcal{L}$ is a complete meet semilattice i.e. each of its non-empty subsets  has a meet (greatest lower boind).
nodes.statement_short: Rootoidal: Phi_g empty forces g=1, the weak order is a complete meet semilattice, and the join-theorem property (JTP) holds.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I

nodes.name: complete signed group-set
nodes.statement: A particularly interesting class of rootoidal signed group-sets $(G,\Phi)$ are the complete ones: $(G,\Phi)$ is said to be complete if $\mathcal{L}$ has a maximum element, or equivalently if the weak order of $\mathcal{L}$ is a complete lattice.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I

nodes.name: Euclidean space $V$ and $G=O(V)$
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a real Euclidean space and $G=O(V)$ be the orthogonal group of $V$.

nodes.name: root system $\Phi$ = unit sphere of $V$
nodes.statement: Let $\Phi$ be the unit sphere in $V$, with its natural action by $G\times\{\pm 1\}$.

nodes.name: positive roots from a total ordering of $V$
nodes.statement: Fix a vector-space total ordering $\preceq$ of $V$ and let $\Phi^{+}:=\{\, v\in \Phi\mid v>0\,\}$ and $\Phi^{-}:=-\Phi^{+}$.

nodes.name: Orthogonal group signed group-set is complete rootoidal
nodes.statement: The pair $(G,\Phi)$ defined above is a complete, rootoidal, signed group-set.
conclusions: The pair $(G,\Phi)$ defined above is a complete, rootoidal, signed group-set.
nodes.statement_short: The orthogonal group with the unit sphere as root system and positives from a total order forms a complete rootoidal signed group-set.

nodes.name: Sufficient conditions for a complete rootoidal signed group-set
nodes.statement: To prove the theorem, we shall use the fact that a signed group-set $(G,\Phi)$ with weak order $L$ is a complete rootoidal signed group-set if the following conditions hold: \begin{enumerate}\item[(7)] If $g\in {G}$ with $\Phi_{g}=\emptyset$ then $g=1_{a}$. \item[(8)] $L$ is a complete join semilattice i.e. each of subsets has a join \item[(9)] If $A\in \mathcal{L}$, then $\Phi^{+}\setminus A\in \mathcal{L}$.
assumptions: $L$ is a complete join  semilattice i.e. each of  subsets  has a join
conclusions: a signed group-set  $(G,\Phi)$ with weak order $L$ is a complete rootoidal signed group-set
nodes.statement_short: A signed group-set is complete rootoidal if Phi_g empty forces g=1, the weak order is a complete join semilattice, and complements stay in L.

nodes.name: Proof of the sufficient conditions
nodes.statement: Indeed, (8) and (9) imply that $L$ is a complete meet semi-lattice by duality. To prove that the JTP holds, let $A_{i}$, $B$ be as in its statement. By (9), $A_{i}\subseteq \Phi^{+}\setminus B\in \mathcal{L}$ for all $i$, so by definition of join, $A=\bigvee A_{i}\subseteq \Phi^{+}\setminus B$ and $A\cap B=\emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: Duality gives complete meets from (8),(9); JTP follows since each A_i lies in the complement of B, which is in L.

nodes.name: set difference $X\backslash Y$
nodes.statement: If $X$ and $Y$ are sets with $Y \subseteq X$, we use $X\backslash Y$ to denote the set $\{x \in X | x \not\in Y\}$.

nodes.name: partially ordered set (poset)
nodes.statement: A partially ordered set or poset is a set $P$ equipped with a binary relation $\leq$ such that for all $x, y, $ and $z \in P$, \begin{enumerate} \item $x \leq x$, \item $x \leq y$ and $y \leq x$ imply $x = y$, \item $x \leq y$ and $y \leq z$ imply $x \leq z$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.genus: set $P$ equipped with a binary relation $\leq$

nodes.name: totally ordered poset
nodes.statement: A poset $P$ with binary operation $\leq$ is totally ordered if given any pair of elements $\{x, y \} \in P$ we have either $x \leq y$ or $y \leq x$.

nodes.name: order isomorphism
nodes.statement: Two posets $P$ and $Q$ are said to be {\bf order isomorphic} if there exists a map $\phi$ from $P$ onto $Q$ such that $x \leq y$ in $P$ if and only if $\phi(x) \leq \phi(y)$ in $Q$. Such a map $\phi$ is called an order isomorphism from $P$ to $Q$.
differentia: $x \leq y$ in $P$ if and only if  $\phi(x) \leq \phi(y)$ in $Q$

nodes.name: dual poset $P^{\delta}$
nodes.statement: Given a partially ordered set $P$ with order relation $\leq_{P}$, its dual, $P^{\delta}$, is the poset which is equal to $P$ as a set, with binary relation $\leq_{P^{\delta}}$ given by $x \leq_{P^{\delta}} y$ if and only if $y \leq_{P} x$.

nodes.name: upper bound
nodes.statement: Given a poset $P$ and a subset $S \subseteq P$, an element $x \in P$ is an {\bf upper bound} for $S$ if $y \leq x$ for all $y \in S$.

nodes.name: least upper bound
nodes.statement: An element $l \in P$ is a {\bf least upper bound} for $S$ if $l$ is an upper bound for $S$ and if $x$ is another upper bound for $S$, then $l \leq x$.

nodes.name: join notation $\bigvee S$
nodes.statement: The least upper bound of the set $S$ is denoted by $\bigvee S$ when it exists or $\bigvee_P S$ if it is unclear which poset we are considering.

nodes.name: binary join $x \vee y$
nodes.statement: In the case of two elements, we let $x \vee y$ denote the least upper bound of the two element set $\{x, y\}$.

nodes.name: lower bounds, greatest lower bounds, $\bigwedge S$, $x\wedge y$
nodes.statement: {\bf Lower bounds } and {\bf greatest lower bounds} are defined dually with $\bigwedge S$ denoting the greatest lower bound of the set $S$ and $x \wedge y$ denoting the greatest lower bound of the set $\{x, y\}$.

nodes.name: lattice and complete lattice
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a non-empty poset. If $x\wedge y$ and $x \vee y$ exist in $P$ for all $x, y \in P$, we say $P$ is a {\bf Lattice}. If $\bigwedge S$ and $\bigvee S$ exist in $P$ for every subset $S$ of $P$, then we say $P$ is a {\bf complete lattice}.
differentia:
$\bigwedge S$ and $\bigvee S$ exist in $P$ 
for every subset  $S$ of $P$

nodes.name: directed set
nodes.statement: If $S$ is a non-empty subset of a poset $P$, $S$ is said to be {\bf directed} if for every pair of elements $x, y \in S$, there exists $z \in S$, such that $z$ is an upper bound for the set $\{x, y\}$.
differentia:
for every pair of elements $x, y \in S$, there exists $z \in S$, such that $z$ is an
upper bound for the set $\{x, y\}$

nodes.name: Euclidean space $\Bbb{R}^{n+1}$ with standard basis
nodes.statement: We let $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ denote The Euclidean $(n + 1)$ space, with standard basis $\{e_1, e_2, \dots , e_{n + 1}\}$.

nodes.name: standard inner product $< , >$
nodes.statement: The standard inner product or dot product on $\Bbb{R}^{n+1}$ is denoted by $< , >$.

nodes.name: unit sphere $S^n$ and positive roots $\Phi_n^+$
nodes.statement: The unit sphere in $\Bbb{R}^{n+1}$ is $$S^n = \{(x_1, x_2, \dots , x_{n+1}) \in \Bbb{R}^{n+1} | x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \dots + x_{n+1}^2 = 1\}$$ and $\Phi_n^+$ is used to denote the set $$\Phi_n^+ = \{(x_1, x_2, \dots , x_{n + 1}) \in S^n | x_m = <x, e_m> > 0 \ \ \mbox{where} \ \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | x_i \not= 0\} \}.$$
nodes.statement_short: S^n is the unit sphere; Phi_n^+ is the set of unit vectors whose last nonzero coordinate is positive.

nodes.name: negative roots $\Phi_n^-$
nodes.statement: For its negative $ -\Phi_n^+ $, we use $$\Phi_n^- = \{(x_1, x_2, \dots , x_{n + 1}) \in S^n | x_m = <x, e_m> < 0 \ \ \mbox{where} \ \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | x_i \not= 0\} \}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Phi_n^- is the set of unit vectors whose last nonzero coordinate is negative.

nodes.name: orthogonal group $O(V)$
nodes.statement: For a Euclidean space $V$, we let $O(V)$ denote the orthogonal group of $V$.

nodes.name: $O_k$
nodes.statement: Sometimes we use $O_{k}$ to denote the orthogonal transformations of $\Bbb{R}^{k}$.

nodes.name: orthogonal complement and orthogonal sum $V = V_1 \bot V_2$
nodes.statement: If $V_1$ and $V_2$ are subspaces of $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $V_1 + V_2 = V$ and $<v_1, v_2> = 0$ for all $v_1 \in V_1$ and $v_2 \in V_2$, then we say that $V_2$ is the orthogonal complement of $V_1$ in $V$ and we write the sum as $V = V_1 \bot V_2$.

nodes.name: orthogonal sum of transformations $T_1 \bot T_2$
nodes.statement: If $T_1 \in O(V_1)$ and $T_2 \in O(V_2)$ and $V = V_1 \bot V_2$, the linear transformation $T = T_1 \bot T_2$ is the unique linear transformation in $O(V)$ with the property that $T(v_1) = T_1(v_1)$ and $T(v_2) = T_2(v_2)$ for all $v_1 \in V_1$ and $v_2 \in V_2$.

nodes.name: identity maps $I_V$ and $1_{e_i}$
nodes.statement: We let $I_V$ denote the identity transformation on $V$ and we let $1_{e_i}$ denote the identity transformation on the subspace $\Bbb{R}e_i$ of $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$.

nodes.name: natural imbedding of $\Bbb{R}^k$ in $\Bbb{R}^{n+1}$
nodes.statement: We have a natural imbedding of $\Bbb{R}^{k}, k < n$ in $R^{n + 1}$ where we identify $\Bbb{R}^{k}$ with the set $\{(x_1, x_2, \dots , x_{n + 1} )| x_m = 0 \ \mbox{if} \ m > k \}$. This induces an imbedding of $S^{k - 1}, \Phi_{k - 1}^+$ and $\Phi_{k - 1}^-$ in $R^{n + 1}$.

nodes.name: topological closure $\bar{X}$
nodes.statement: The topological closure of a set $X \subseteq \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with respect to the metric defined by this norm on $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ is denoted by $\bar{X}$.

nodes.name: cone, convex cone, pointed convex cone
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product $<- , ->$. A subset $C \subseteq V$ is called a {\bf cone} if $C$ satisfies conditions (1) and (2) below: \begin{enumerate} \item $0 \in C$, \item If $v \in C$, then $\Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}v \subseteq C$. \noindent \leftline{C is called a {\bf convex cone} if it also satisfies the property:} \item If $u, v \in C$, then $u + v \in C$. \noindent A convex cone $C$ is a {\bf pointed convex cone} if it is a convex cone and satisfies the property: \item $C \cap (-C) = \{0\}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Cones contain 0 and are closed under nonnegative scaling; convex cones are closed under addition; pointed ones meet their negative only at 0.
nodes.origin_citation: Fenchel, Convex cones, sets, and functions
nodes.label: cones

nodes.name: ray $(x)$
nodes.statement: Note that for any cone $C$ contained in $R^k$, $k > 0$, if $x \not= 0 \in C$, the {\bf ray} $(x) = \{rx | r \in \Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}\}$ is contained in $C$.

nodes.name: rays in a cone correspond to points on the sphere
nodes.statement: This ray intersects the unit sphere $S^{k - 1}$ at exactly one point $\frac{x}{||x||}$. Thus we have a one to one correspondence between the rays in $C$ and the points on the unit sphere $S^{k - 1}$ which are in $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Each ray meets the unit sphere once, giving a bijection between rays of C and points of C on the sphere.

nodes.name: cone $\widehat{X}$ over a subset of the sphere
nodes.statement: Let $X \subseteq S^n$, we use $\widehat{X}$ to denote the following cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$: $$\widehat{X} = \{rx | x \in X \ \mbox{and} \ r \in \Bbb{R}_{\geq 0} \} \ \mbox{if} \ X \not= \emptyset$$ and $\widehat{\emptyset} = \{0\}$.
nodes.label: hatconedef

nodes.name: Cone over a subset of the sphere
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be subsets of $S^n$. \begin{enumerate} \item $X = \widehat{X} \cap S^n$ and if $C$ is any cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = C\cap S^n$, then $\widehat{X} = C$, \item $X\cap Y = \emptyset$, if and only if $\widehat{X} \cap \widehat{Y} = \{0\}$. \end{enumerate}
conclusions:
$X = \widehat{X} \cap S^n$ and   if 
$C$ is any cone  in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = C\cap S^n$, then $\widehat{X} = C$,
$X\cap Y = \emptyset$, if and only if  $\widehat{X} \cap \widehat{Y} = \{0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: X-hat is the unique cone whose trace on the sphere is X; disjoint subsets give cones meeting only at 0.
nodes.label: hatcone

nodes.statement:
Assertion (1) is trivial if $X = \emptyset$, so let us assume for now that $X 
ot= \emptyset$. We have $\widehat{X}$ is a union of rays, $\widehat{X} =  igcup_{x \in X, x 
ot= 0} (x)$. Since each ray $(x)$ where $x \in X$ cuts the unit sphere exactly once at $x$, we have $X = \widehat{X} \cap S^n$. If C is a cone with $C \cap S^n = X$, then $\widehat{X} \subseteq C$, since the entire ray $(x)$ is in $C$ if $x \in X$. On the other hand, if $c \in C$, the ray $(c)$ cuts the sphere $S^n$ at $ rac{c}{||c||} \in X$. Therefore $( rac{c}{||c||}) = (c) \in \widehat{X}$ and since $C$ is the union of such rays, we have $C \subseteq \widehat{X}$. This proves (1). We can now relax the assumption that $X 
ot= \emptyset$. It is easily seen that $\widehat{X} \cap \widehat{Y} = \widehat{X \cap Y}$. Assertion (2) follows from the observation that if $C$ is a cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$, then $C \cap S^n = \emptyset$ if and only if $C = \{0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct: write X-hat as a union of rays, each meeting the sphere once; (2) from X-hat cap Y-hat = (X cap Y)-hat.

nodes.name: Closure commutes with intersection with the sphere
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$, then $\overline{A \cap S^{n} } = \bar{A} \cap S^n$.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$
conclusions: $\overline{A \cap S^{n} } = \bar{A} \cap S^n$.
nodes.label: cone

nodes.statement: Let $A \subset \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ be a convex cone. Since $ \bar{A} \cap S^n$ is closed and contains $A \cap S^{n}$, we have $\overline{A \cap S^{n} } \subseteq \bar{A} \cap S^n$. On the other hand, if $x \in \bar{A} \cap S^n$, then $||x|| = 1$ and we have a sequence of points $\{x_i\}_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ in $A$ such that $\lim_{i \to \infty}x_i = x$. Since $A$ is convex we have the sequence of points $\{\frac{x_i}{||x_i||}\}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \in \bar{A} \cap S^n$. Given any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $m$ such that $| ||x_i|| - 1 | = | ||x_i|| - ||x|| | \leq ||x_i - x|| < \epsilon $ for all $i \geq m$. Since $$||x - \frac{x_i}{||x_i||}|| \leq ||x - x_i|| + ||x_i - \frac{x_i}{||x_i||}|| = ||x - x_i|| + \frac{||x_i||(| \ ||x_i|| - 1|)}{||x_i||} \leq 2\epsilon$$ for $i \geq m$, we have that the sequence $\{\frac{x_i}{||x_i||}\}_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ converges to $x$ and $x \in \overline{A \cap S^{n} }$.
nodes.statement_short: Double inclusion; normalize an approximating sequence and bound its distance to x.

nodes.name: closed half space, hyperplane, open half space
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product $<- , ->$. For any fixed $u \in V$, we let $H_u$ denote {\bf the closed half space} $H_u = \{v \in V | <v, u> \leq 0 \}$. We let $H(u)$ denote the {\bf hyperplane} $\{ v \in V | <v, u> = 0 \}$ and we let $H_u^{int}$ denote the {\bf open half space } $\{ v \in V | <v, u> < 0 \}$. \\ We will use the notation $H^V_u, H^V(u)$, and $H^{Vint}_u$ when we want to emphasize the underlying vector space.\\

nodes.name: Half spaces and hyperplanes determined by normals
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$. If $u, v \in V$ with $H(u) \subseteq H_v$, then $H(u) = H(v)$. Consequently if $u, v \in V$ with $H_u \subseteq H_v$, then $H_u = H_v$. Also $v_1 = \frac{-v}{||v||} \in H_v$ is the unique vector of norm one in $H_v$ with the property that $H_{v} = H_{-v_1}$.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$.
conclusions:
Consequently if  $u, v \in V$ with
  $H_u \subseteq H_v$, then $H_u = H_v$.
Also  $v_1 = \frac{-v}{||v||}  \in H_v$ is the unique vector of norm one in $H_v$ with the property that $H_{v} = H_{-v_1}$.
nodes.statement_short: A hyperplane inside a closed half space is its boundary; nested half spaces are equal; the unit inward normal is unique.
nodes.label: hyper

nodes.statement: Suppose $u, v \in V$ with $H(u) \subseteq H_v = \{x \in V | <x, v> \leq 0 \}$. If $x \in H(u)$ with the property that $<x, v> \not= 0$, then $\{x,-x\} \in H(u)$ and either $<x, v> > 0$ or $<-x, v> > 0$ giving a contradiction. Hence $H(u) \subseteq H(v)$ and we have equality by comparing dimensions. If $H_u \subseteq H_v$, then $H(u) \subseteq H_v$ and therefore $H(u) = H(v)$. Now $V = <v> \bot H(v) = <u> \bot H(u) = <u> \bot H(v)$ and $u = cv$. Since $H_u \subseteq H_v$, $-u \in H_v$, hence $<-u, v> = <-cv, v> < 0$ and we have $c > 0$. Therefore $H_u = H_v$. Let $v_1 \in H_v$ such that $H_{-v_1} = H_{v}$, then as above, $-v_1 = cv$ for some $c > 0$. If we assume $||v_1|| = 1$, then we must have $v_1 = \frac{-v}{||v||} $.
nodes.statement_short: Direct: a vector off H(v) and its negative cannot both lie in H_v; then compare normals via orthogonal decompositions.

nodes.name: Two open half spaces intersect
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$ and let $u, v \in V$. Then $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}$ is non-empty if $ u \not= -cv, \ c > 0$.
conclusions: $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}$ is non-empty if $ u \not= -cv, \ c > 0$.
nodes.label: halfspaceintersect

nodes.statement: Let $u, v \in V$. Clearly $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int} = \emptyset$ if $u = -cv$ for some $c > 0$ in $\Bbb{R}$. Lets assume that $u \not= -cv, c > 0$. Suppose that $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int} = \emptyset$, then if $x \in H_u^{int}$ we must have $x \not\in H_v^{int}$ and $<x, v> \geq 0$ and $H_u^{int} \subseteq H_{-v}$. Taking closures, we get $H_u \subseteq H_{-v}$ and by Lemma \ref{hyper} $H_u = H_{-v}$ and $u = -cv$ for some $c > 0$ giving us a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: an empty intersection forces H_u inside H_{-v}, hence u = -cv by Lemma 3.6.

nodes.name: Closure of intersection of open half spaces
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$ and let $u, v \in V$ for which $ u \not= -cv, \ c > 0$. Then $$\overline{H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}} = H_u \cap H_v.$$
assumptions: let $u, v \in V$ for which $ u \not= -cv, \ c > 0$.
conclusions: $$\overline{H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}} = H_u \cap H_v.$$
nodes.label: closure

nodes.statement:
Let $u$ and $v$ be as in the statement of the lemma and let $C = H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}$. Clearly the lemma is true if $u = cv$ for some $c > 0$. Therefore we will assume that $u 
ot= cv$ for any $c \in \Bbb{R}$ for the rest of the proof. In this case $H(u) 
ot= H(v)$. Since $\overline{H_u^{int}} = H_u$ and $\overline{H_v^{int}} = H_v$, we have $C \subseteq H_{u} \cap H_{v}$ and since $H_{u} \cap H_{v}$ is a closed set, we have $ ar{C} \subseteq H_{u} \cap H_{v}$. To verify the opposite inclusion, consider $x \in H_{u} \cap H_v$. If $x \in C$, then $x \in  ar{C}$. Therefore we need only consider points $x$ where $<x, u> = 0$ or $<x, v> = 0$ or both. If $<x, u> = 0$ and $<x, v> > 0$, we have a sequence $\{x_i\}_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ in $H_{u}^{int}$ with $\lim_{i 	o \infty} x_i = x$. Now since $x \in H_{v}^{int}$ which is an open set, there exists an $m$ for which $x_i \in H_{v}^{int}$ for all $i \geq m$. Therefore $x_i \in C$ for all $i \geq m$ and $x \in  ar{C}$. A similar argument shows that if $<x, v> = 0$ and $<x, u> < 0$, we have $x \in  ar{C}$. Now if $<x, v> = 0$ and $<x, u> = 0$, then $x \in [H(u) \cap H(v)]$ which is a subspace of $H(v)$ of dimension $n - 2$ since $H(u) 
ot= H(v)$. Let $H = [H(u) \cap H(v)]$. It remains to show that $H \subseteq  ar{C}$. We consider $H$ as a hyperplane in $H(v)$. It is not difficult to see that if $y \in H(v)$, $<y, u> = < y, \pi(u)>$ where $\pi(u)$ is the orthogonal projection of $u$ onto the hyperplane $H(v)$. Therefore $$H = \{y \in H(v) | <y, \pi(u)> = 0 \} = H^{H(v)}(\pi(u))$$ as a hyperplane in $H(v)$. Now looking at the corresponding open half space in $H(v)$, we have $H_{\pi(u)}^{H(v){int}} = \{x \in H(v)| <x,\pi(u)> < 0\}$. By our reasoning above we know this is a subset of $ ar{C}$. Taking the closure within $H(v)$, we have $H^{H(v)}_{\pi(u)} = \overline{H_{\pi(u)}^{H(v)int} }\subseteq  ar{C}$ and $H = H^{H(v)}(\pi(u)) \subseteq  ar{C}$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Double inclusion with case analysis on which boundary hyperplanes contain x. The codimension-two part is handled by viewing it as a hyperplane in H(v) and projecting u.

nodes.name: maximal pointed convex cone
nodes.statement: A pointed convex cone $D$ in a Euclidean space $V$ is called {\bf maximal} if $D \cap (-D) = \{0\}$ and $D \cup (-D) = V$.

nodes.name: maximal pointed convex cones define total orderings
nodes.statement: Note that a maximal pointed convex cone in a Euclidean space $V$ defines a total ordering on $V$ given by $y \leq x$ if and only if $y - x \in D$. Also $D = \{v \in V | v \leq 0\}$.

nodes.name: support of a cone
nodes.statement: A closed half space $H_u$ is called a {\bf support for a cone} $C$ if $C \subseteq H_u$.
nodes.origin_citation: Fenchel, Convex cones, sets, and functions

nodes.name: Unique support of a maximal pointed convex cone
nodes.statement: Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in a Euclidean space $V$ with positive definite inner product $<-, - >$. Then $D$ has a unique support $H_v$, in $V$ and $H_v = \bar{D}$. Furthermore $H_v^{int} = \{x \in V | <x, v> < 0 \} \subset D$.
assumptions: Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in a Euclidean space $V$  with  positive definite inner product $<-, - >$.
conclusions: $D$ has a unique support  $H_v$,  in $V$ and $H_v = \bar{D}$.
Furthermore  $H_v^{int} = \{x \in V | <x, v> < 0 \} \subset D$.
nodes.statement_short: A maximal pointed convex cone has a unique supporting half space, equal to its closure and containing the open half space.
nodes.label: unique

nodes.statement: According to Corollary 1 to Theorem 1 of Fenchel \cite{Fenchel}, a maximal pointed convex cone $D$ in $V$, has a support $H_{v}$, where $D \subseteq H_{v}$. Now since $D \cup (-D) = V$ we have $H_v^{int} = \{x \in V | <x, v> < 0 \} \subseteq D$. Otherwise we would have $x \in (-D)$ with $<x, v> < 0$ and thus $<-x, v> > 0$ for $-x \in D$ giving us a contradiction. Thus we have $\overline{H_v^{int}} = H_{v} \subseteq \bar{D}$. On the other hand $\bar{D} \subseteq H_{v}$ since $D \subseteq H_{v}$, therefore $\bar{D} = H_v$. Suppose that $H_{u}$ is also a support. Then as above, we have $\bar{D} = H_u$ and hence $H_u = H_v$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a support from Fenchel's corollary; maximality puts the open half space inside D, so the closure equals the support, forcing uniqueness.

nodes.name: Maximal pointed convex cones correspond to ordered orthonormal bases
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a finite dimensional Euclidean space of dimension $n$ with positive definite inner product $< - , - >$. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item D is a maximal pointed convex cone in V, \item There exists an ordered basis $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ of $V$ with $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_i \in \Bbb{R}, c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\},$$ \item There exists an ordered orthonormal basis $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ of $V$ with $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_i \in \Bbb{R}, c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$ \end{enumerate} Moreover the map taking $D$ to $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ is a bijection from the maximal pointed convex cones in $V$ to the set of ordered orthonormal bases of $V$. The orthogonal group $O(V)$ acts simply transitively on the set of maximal pointed convex cones in $V$.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a finite dimensional Euclidean  space of dimension $n$ with positive definite inner product $< - , - >$.
conclusions: Moreover the map taking $D$ to $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ is a bijection from the maximal pointed convex cones in $V$ to the set of  ordered  orthonormal bases of $V$.
The orthogonal  group $O(V)$ acts simply transitively on the set of maximal pointed convex cones in $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Maximal pointed convex cones are exactly lexicographic negative cones of ordered (orthonormal) bases; they biject with ordered orthonormal bases, with a simply transitive O(V)-action.
nodes.label: equivalence

nodes.statement:
The result is obvious if $n = 1$, since the only maximal pointed convex cones of $\Bbb{R}e_1$ are $\Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}e_1$ and $\Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}(-e_1)$. We use induction on the dimension of $V$. Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in $V$. From Theorem ef{unique} we know that $D$ has a unique support $H_{v_{n }}$, where $D \subseteq H_{v_{n }}$ and $H_{v_n}^{int} \subseteq D$. From Lemma ef{hyper} we know that we can choose a $v_n$ which is unique with the property that $-v_n \in D$, $||v_n|| = 1$ and $D \subseteq H_{v_{n }}$. Now consider the set $\widetilde{D} = D \cap H(v_{n })$. It is not difficult to see that $\widetilde{D}$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $H(v_{n })$. By induction, we get an orthonormal basis $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n - 1 }\}$ for $H(v_{n })$ such that $$\widetilde{D} = \{x \in H(v_{n }) | <x, v_m> < 0 \ \mbox{for} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | <x, v_m> 
ot= 0\}, 1\leq i \leq n -1 \} \cup \{0\}.$$ Now $D = \{x \in V | <x, v_{n }> < 0\} \cup \widetilde{D}$ and $$D = \{x \in V | <x, v_m> < 0 \ \mbox{for} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | <x, v_m> 
ot= 0\} , 1\leq i \leq n \} \cup \{0\}$$ where $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n\}$ is an orthonormal basis for $V$. This proves that (1) implies (3). That (3) implies (2) is trivial. To show that (2) implies (1), let $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ be an ordered basis of $V$ and let $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$ It is trivial to check that $D$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $V$. Therefore (2) implies (1). Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in $V$ with $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\} $$ where $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $V$. Suppose $\{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_n\}$ is another orthonormal basis of $V$ for which $$D = \{c_1u_1 + c_2u_2 + \dots + c_nu_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}. $$ We have both $H_{u_n}$ and $H_{v_n}$ are supporting half spaces for $D$. Therefore, by Theorem ef{unique} we have $H_{u_n} = H_{v_n}$ and since $||u_n|| = ||v_n|| = 1$, by Lemma ef{hyper}, $u_n = v_n$. Now $ \{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_{n-1} \}$ and $ \{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n-1} \}$ are ordered orthonormal bases of $H = H(u_n) = H(v_n)$ and $\widetilde{D} = D \cap H $ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $H$ with $$\widetilde{D} = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_{n- 1}v_{n-1} | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}$$ $$= \{c_1u_1 + c_2u_2 + \dots + c_{n- 1}u_{n-1} | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$ Hence by induction, we have $ \{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_{n-1} \}$ and $ \{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n-1} \}$ are equal as ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and hence $ \{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_{n-1}, u_n \}$ and\ $ \{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n-1}, v_n \}$ are equal as ordered orthonormal bases of $V$. This shows that the map taking maximal pointed convex cones to ordered orthonormal bases given above is one to one. The map is onto since (3) implies (1). Since the orthogonal group $O(V)$ acts simply transitively on the set of ordered orthonormal bases of $V$, and by linearity the action commutes with the above map from ordered orthonormal bases to maximal pointed convex cones in $V$, we have a simple transitive action of $O(V)$ on the set of maximal pointed convex cones in $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on dim V. The unique support (Thm 3.11) gives the last basis vector, and the cone restricted to the hyperplane is again maximal.

nodes.name: the poset $\mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: For $n \geq 0$ we let $\mathcal{L}_n$ denote the following poset of subsets of $S^n$ ordered by inclusion: $$\mathcal{L}_n = \{T(\Phi^-_n) \cap \Phi_n^+ | T\in O_{n + 1} \} .$$
nodes.genus: poset of subsets of $S^n$ ordered by inclusion
nodes.statement_short: L_n is the set of all T(Phi_n^-) cap Phi_n^+ for T orthogonal, ordered by inclusion (the weak order of O_{n+1}).

nodes.name: $\Phi_n^+$ is the maximum of $\mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: Note that $\Phi_n^+ = T(\Phi^-_n)\cap \Phi_n^+$ when $T = -I_{\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}}$. This is a maximal element of $\mathcal{L}_n$.

nodes.name: cone $D_T$ of an orthogonal transformation
nodes.statement: If $T \in O_{n + 1}$ with $T(e_i) = v_i$, $1 \leq i \leq n + 1$, we let $$D_T = \{ v = \sum_{i = 1}^{n + 1}c_iv_i \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1} | <v, v_m> = c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where } \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0\}\} \cup \{0\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: D_T is the set of vectors whose last nonzero coordinate in the basis T(e_i) is negative, plus 0.

nodes.name: $D_T$ is a maximal pointed convex cone
nodes.statement: It is not difficult to show that $D_T $ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $D_T \cap S^{n} = T(\Phi_n^-)$.
conclusions:
$D_T $ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with 
$D_T \cap S^{n} =  T(\Phi_n^-)$

nodes.name: Unique maximal pointed convex cone of an element of $\mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$, then there is a unique maximal pointed convex cone $D_X = D_{T_X}$ in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with the property that $X = D_X \cap \Phi_n^+$.
conclusions:
there is a unique maximal 
pointed convex   cone 
$D_X = D_{T_X}$ in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with the property that $X = D_X \cap \Phi_n^+$.
nodes.label: mpcc

nodes.statement: From its definition, we have that $D_{T_X}$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $D_{T_X} \cap \Phi_n^+ = T_X(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+ = X$. Suppose that $D$ is another maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = D \cap \Phi_n^+$. If $D_e = D_{-I_{\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}}}$, then $\Phi_n^+ = D_e \cap S^n$ and $X = D_X \cap D_e \cap S^n = D \cap D_e \cap S^n$. Now $C_1 = D_X \cap D_e$ and $C_2 = D \cap D_e$ are both convex cones in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = C_1 \cap S^n = C_2 \cap S^n$. By Lemma \ref{hatcone}, $\hat{X} = C_1 = C_2$. Let $C'_1 = (D_e \backslash C_1) \cup \{0\} = D_e \cap (-D_X)$. Now $$[C_1 \cup (-C'_1) ] \cup [C'_1 \cup (-C_1)] = D_e \cup (-D_e) = \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$$ and $$[C_1 \cup (-C'_1) ] \cap [C'_1 \cup (-C_1)] = \{0\}$$ since $C_1 \cup (-C'_1) \subseteq D_X$ and $C'_1 \cup (-C_1) \subseteq -D_X$. Since $D_X \cap [C'_1 \cup (-C_1)] = \{0\}$, we can conclude that $D_X = C_1 \cup (-C'_1)$. Since $C'_1 = (D_e \backslash C_2) \cup \{0\} = D_e \cap (-D)$, we can similarly conclude that $D = C_1 \cup (-C'_1)$ and hence $D = D_X$.
nodes.statement_short: Existence from D_T; uniqueness by recovering D_X from its intersection with D_e and its complement in D_e via Lemma 3.3.

nodes.name: $D_e$ and $D_X$
nodes.statement: We define $D_e = D_{-I_{\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}}}$, that is $$D_e = \{ x = \sum_{i = 1}^{n + 1}c_ie_i \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1} | <x, e_m> = c_m > 0 \ \mbox{where } \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0\}\} \cup \{0\}$$ and $D_e \cap S^n = \Phi_n^+$. For $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$ we let $D_X$ denote the unique maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ for which $X = D_X \cap \Phi_n^+ = D_X \cap D_e \cap S^n$.
nodes.statement_short: D_e is the positive lexicographic cone (D_{-I}) with D_e cap S^n = Phi_n^+; D_X is the unique maximal pointed convex cone with X = D_X cap Phi_n^+.
nodes.label: mpccX

nodes.name: characterization of $\mathcal{L}_n$ via maximal pointed convex cones
nodes.statement: Therefore we can characterize $\mathcal{L}_n$ as $$\mathcal{L}_n = \{D\cap \Phi_n^+ | D \ \mbox{is a maximal pointed convex cone in } \ \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}\}.$$
conclusions: $$\mathcal{L}_n = \{D\cap \Phi_n^+ | D \ \mbox{is a maximal pointed convex cone in } \ \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: L_n consists exactly of the traces D cap Phi_n^+ of maximal pointed convex cones D.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{L}_0$
nodes.statement: If $n = 0$, then $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1} = \Bbb{R}^1 = \Bbb{R}e_1$. We have $S^0 = \{-e_1, e_1\}, \Phi_0^+ = \{e_1\}$ and $O_1 = \{\pm 1_{e_1}\}$. Therefore $\mathcal{L}_0 = \{\emptyset, \{e_1\}\}$.

nodes.name: Duality of $\mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, then $\Phi^+_n \backslash X$ is also an element of $\mathcal{L}_n$. The map $\phi: \mathcal{L}_n \to \mathcal{L}_n^{\delta}$ given by $\phi(X) = \Phi^+_n \backslash X$ is an order isomorphism of posets.
conclusions: $\Phi^+_n \backslash X$ is also an element of $\mathcal{L}_n$.

The map $\phi: \mathcal{L}_n \to \mathcal{L}_n^{\delta}$ given by 
$\phi(X) = \Phi^+_n \backslash X$ is an order  isomorphism of posets.
nodes.statement_short: Complementation in Phi_n^+ preserves L_n and is an order isomorphism onto the dual poset.
nodes.label: duality

nodes.statement: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$. There exists a maximal pointed convex cone $D$ in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ for which $X = D \cap \Phi_n^+$. We have that $(-D)$ is also a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ and $(-D)\cap \Phi_n^+ = \Phi_n^+ \backslash X$. Hence $\Phi_n^+ \backslash X \in \mathcal{L}_n$. Since $\phi^2(X) = X$, it is easy to see that $\phi$ is a bijective map. Since $ \Phi_n^+ \backslash X \subseteq \Phi_n^+ \backslash Y$ if and only if $X \supseteq Y$, we have an isomorphism of posets $\phi: \mathcal{L}_n \to \mathcal{L}_n^{\delta}$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace D by -D to get the complement; complementation is an order-reversing involution.

nodes.name: Restriction of elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$ to $\Bbb{R}^n$
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an element of $\mathcal{L}_n$, then $X \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }$ is an element of $\mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$, where $\Bbb{R}^n $ is imbedded in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1} $ as in Section \ref{intro}.
conclusions:
$X \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }$ is an 
element of $\mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$
nodes.label: projection

nodes.statement: Given $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, we have a maximal pointed convex cone $D \subset \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ such that $X = D \cap \Phi_n^+$. Let $\widetilde{D} = D \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }$. It is not difficult to see that $\widetilde{D}$ is a maximal pointed convex cone of $\Bbb{R}^{n }$ and therefore $X \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } = D \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+ = \widetilde{D} \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+ \in \mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Intersect the maximal pointed convex cone D with R^n, which is again maximal.

nodes.name: Boundary description of elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $X = T_X(\Phi^-_n)\cap \Phi^+_n$ for some $T_X \in O_{n + 1}$. Let $u_X = T_X(e_{n + 1})$ and $e = -e_{n + 1}$. If $u_X \not= e_{n + 1} = -e$, then \begin{enumerate} \item $X = (X\cap H(u_X)) \cup \{x \in \Phi_n^+ | <x, u_X> < 0 \},$ \item $\bar{X} = [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}] \cap S^n$, \item $\bar{X} \cap S^{n -1} = H_{u_X}\cap S^{n - 1} \supseteq H(u_X)\cap S^{n - 1}$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $X = T_X(\Phi^-_n)\cap \Phi^+_n$ for some $T_X \in O_{n + 1}$.
conclusions: $X = (X\cap H(u_X)) \cup \{x \in \Phi_n^+ | <x, u_X> < 0 \},$
$\bar{X} =  [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}] \cap S^n$,
$\bar{X} \cap S^{n -1} = H_{u_X}\cap S^{n - 1} \supseteq H(u_X)\cap S^{n - 1}$.
nodes.statement_short: An element X of L_n splits along the hyperplane H(u_X), and its closure is the sphere's intersection with two closed half spaces.
nodes.label: boundary

nodes.statement: (1) follows from the fact that $X = T_X(\Phi^-_n) \cap \Phi^+_n$ and that $$ T_X(\Phi_n^-) = \{x \in S^n| x = \sum_{i = 1}^{n + 1}c_iT_X(e_i) \ \mbox{such that } \ c_m < 0 , \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i| c_i \not= 0\}\}.$$ Assertion (3) follows from (2) since, given (2), we have $$\bar{X}\cap S^{n -1} = [H_{u_X}\cap S^{n - 1}] \cap [H_{e} \cap S^{n - 1}] \cap [S^n \cap S^{n - 1}] = [H_{u_X}\cap S^{n - 1}] \cap S^{n - 1}.$$ It remains to prove (2). Let $C$ be the convex cone $[H_{u_X}^{int} \cap H_{e}^{int}] \cup \{0\}$, the intersection of the two open half spaces with the zero vector attached. $C$ is non-empty by Lemma \ref{halfspaceintersect}. Now $C \cap S^{n} \subset X \subseteq [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n $ and hence $$ \overline{C \cap S^{n} } \subseteq \overline{X} \subseteq [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n .$$ By Lemma \ref{cone} $$\overline{C} \cap S^{n} \subseteq \overline{X} \subseteq [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n. $$ By Lemma \ref{closure}, $\bar{C} = H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}$. Therefore $\overline{X} = [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n$ and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Assertion (1) from the coordinate description of T_X(Phi_n^-); (3) from (2). (2) by sandwiching X between C cap S^n and the half spaces, using Lemmas 3.4, 3.7, 3.8.

nodes.name: Equality of hyperplane traces on $\Bbb{R}^n$
nodes.statement: Let $X$, $Y \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$ and $Y = T_Y(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$. Let $u_X = T_X(e_{n + 1})$ and let $u_Y = T_Y(e_{n + 1})$. If $H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \not= \Bbb{R}^{n }$ and $H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \subseteq H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }$, then $$H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } = H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }.$$
conclusions: $$H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } = H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }.$$
nodes.label: equality

nodes.statement: We have $ H(u_Y)\cap \Bbb{R}^{n } $ is a subspace of $\Bbb{R}^{n}$ of dimension $n$ or of dimension $n - 1$ . Since we are assuming that $H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \not= \Bbb{R}^{n }$, it must be a subspace of dimension $n - 1$. Since $H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^n \subseteq H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^n$ it too must be a subspace of dimension $n - 1$ and hence must be all of $H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Dimension count: both traces are (n-1)-dimensional subspaces, so inclusion forces equality.

nodes.name: Transformations fixing $\Bbb{R}^n$ split
nodes.statement: Let $Z \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $Z = T_Z(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+$ for some $T_Z \in O_{n + 1}$. Let $u_Z = T_Z(e_{n + 1})$. If $H(u_Z) = \Bbb{R}^n$, then $T_Z = T'_Z \bot \pm 1_{e_{n + 1}}$ for some $T'_Z \in O_n$.
assumptions: Let $Z \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $Z = T_Z(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+$ for some $T_Z \in O_{n + 1}$.
conclusions: $T_Z = T'_Z \bot \pm 1_{e_{n + 1}}$ for some $T'_Z \in O_n$.
nodes.label: Z

nodes.statement: Since $T_Z$ is an isometry, with $T_Z(\Bbb{R}^n) = H(u_Z) = \Bbb{R}^n$, we have $T_Z|_{\Bbb{R}^n} = T'_Z \in O_n$. Now $||u_Z|| = 1$ and $<u_Z, x> = 0$ for all $x \in \Bbb{R}^n$. Hence $u_Z = \pm e_{n + 1}$ and $T_Z = T'_Z\bot \pm 1_{e_{n + 1}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct: T_Z preserves R^n, so u_Z is a unit vector orthogonal to R^n.

nodes.name: Joins exist in $\mathcal{L}_0$
nodes.statement: Obviously we can find $X\vee Y$ in $\mathcal{L}_0$ for any pair of elements $\{X, Y\}$ in $\mathcal{L}_0$.
nodes.section: 5 The least upper bound of two elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$.
conclusions:
we can find 
$X\vee Y$ in $\mathcal{L}_0$ for any pair of elements $\{X, Y\}$ in $\mathcal{L}_0$

nodes.name: Upper bounds when hyperplane traces differ
nodes.statement:
Let $X, Y \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$ and $Y = T_Y(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$, where $T_X, T_Y \in O_{n + 1}$. Let $u_X = T_X(e_{n + 1})$ and $u_Y = T_Y(e_{n + 1})$. Assume that $H(u_X) 
ot= \Bbb{R}^{n}$ and $H(u_Y) 
ot= \Bbb{R}^{n}$. Then if $H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n} 
ot= H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n}$ and $Z \in \mathcal{L}_n$ has the property that $X\subseteq Z$ and $Y\subseteq Z$, where $Z = T_Z(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+$ for some $T_Z \in O_{n + 1}$, we must have $$T_Z(\Bbb{R}^{n}) = \Bbb{R}^{n} \ \ \mbox{and} \ \ T_Z = T_Z'  ot (-1_{e_{n + 1}}).$$
nodes.section: 5 The least upper bound of two elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$.
assumptions: Let $X, Y \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$ and $Y = T_Y(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$, where $T_X, T_Y \in O_{n + 1}$.
$Z \in \mathcal{L}_n$ has the property that $X\subseteq Z$ and $Y\subseteq Z$

nodes.statement:
Let $X, Y \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$ and $Y = T_Y(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$, where $T_X, T_Y \in O_{n + 1}$. Let $u_X = T_X(e_{n + 1})$ and let $u_Y = T_Y(e_{n + 1})$. Assume that $H(u_X) 
ot= \Bbb{R}^{n}$ and $H(u_Y) 
ot= \Bbb{R}^{n}$. If $H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n} 
ot= H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n}$ there exists $Z \in \mathcal{L}_{n}$ such that $Z = X \vee Y$.

assumptions: Let $X, Y \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$ and $Y = T_Y(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$, where $T_X, T_Y \in O_{n + 1}$.

nodes.label: OTHER

nodes.statement: Let $X_1 = X \cap \Bbb{R}^n$ and $Y_1 = Y \cap \Bbb{R}^n$. Then by Theorem \ref{projection} we have $X_1 \in \mathcal{L}_{n - 1} $ and $Y_1 \in \mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$. We proceed by induction. Let $Z_1 \in \mathcal{L}_{n -1}$ where $Z_1$ is the least upper bound of $\{X_1, Y_1\} $ in $ \mathcal{L}_{n -1}$. Then $Z_1 = D_{Z_1} \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+$ for a unique maximal pointed convex cone of $\Bbb{R}^n$. Let $D_Z = D_{Z_1} \cup \{x \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1} | <x, e_{n + 1}> > 0\}$. It is not difficult to see that $D_Z$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $D_Z \cap \Bbb{R}^n = D_{Z_1}$. We let $Z = D_Z \cap \Phi_n^+ \in \mathcal{L}_n$. Then $Z\cap S^{n - 1} = Z_1$ and therefore $$X = X_1 \cup [X \cap \{x \in S^n | <x, e_{n + 1}> > 0\}] \subseteq Z$$ and $$Y = Y_1 \cup [Y \cap \{x \in S^n | <x, e_{n + 1}> > 0\}] \subseteq Z.$$ Now, if $W \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with the property that both $X$ and $Y$ are subsets of $W$, then Theorem \ref{conditions} tells us that $\{x \in S^n | <x, e_{n + 1}> > 0\} \subseteq W$. Since $W\cap S^{n - 1}$ contains both $X_1$ and $Y_1$ and, according to Theorem \ref{projection}, $W\cap S^{n - 1} \in \mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$, we must have $Z_1 = Z\cap S^{n - 1} \subset W\cap S^{n - 1} \subseteq W$. Therefore $Z \subseteq W$ and $Z$ is the least upper bound of $\{X, Y\}$ in $\mathcal{L}_n$.

nodes.statement_short: Induction on n: join the restrictions to R^n in L_{n-1} and add the open upper hemisphere; Theorem 5.1 shows it is least.

nodes.name: Join exists when closures are nested
nodes.statement: Let $X, Y \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+$ and $Y = T_Y(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+$. If $\bar{X} \subseteq \bar{Y}$, then there exists $Z \in \mathcal{L}_{n}$ such that $Z$ is the least upper bound of the set $\{X, Y\}$.
nodes.section: 5 The least upper bound of two elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$.
assumptions: Let $X, Y \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+$ and $Y = T_Y(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+$.
conclusions: there exists $Z \in \mathcal{L}_{n}$ such that $Z$ is the least upper bound of the set $\{X, Y\}$.
nodes.label: BAR

nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be as in the statement of the theorem with $\bar{X} \subseteq \bar{Y}$. Then $X = D_X \cap \Phi_n^+$ and $Y = D_X \cap \Phi_n^+$ where $D_X$ and $D_Y$ are maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$. Suppose $Z = T_Z(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+ = D_Z\cap \Phi_n^+ \in \mathcal{L}_n$ is an upper bound for $\{X, Y\}$, where $T_Z \in O_{n + 1}$ and $D_Z$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$. Now $Z = X \vee Y$ if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are contained in $Z$ and if $D_1$ is any maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ for which $X$ and $Y$ are contained in $D_1 \cap \Phi^+_n$, then $Z = D_Z \cap \Phi^+_n \subseteq D_1 \cap \Phi^+_n$. We will use this characterization of $X\vee Y$ and induction on $n$ to show that $Z = X\vee Y$ exists in $\mathcal{L}_n$. We have already noted that we can find the join of any two elements in $\mathcal{L}_0$. Let $u_Y = T_Y(e_{n + 1})$ and recall the definition of $D_e$ from Definition \ref{mpccX}. We first work on constructing that part of the boundary of $Z$ which meets $H(u_Y)$. Let $$\dddot{\Phi} = \Phi_n^+ \cap H(u_Y) = D_e \cap H(u_y) \cap S^{n} = \dddot{D_e}\cap S^{n },$$ where $\dddot{D_e} = D_e \cap H(u_y)$. We let $$\dddot{X} = X \cap H(u_Y) = D_X \cap H(u_Y) \cap \Phi_n^+ = \dddot{D_X} \cap \Phi_n^+ = \dddot{D_X} \cap \dddot{\Phi}$$ where $\dddot{D_X} = D_X \cap H(u_Y)$ and let $$\dddot{Y} = Y \cap H(u_Y) =D_Y \cap H(u_Y) \cap \Phi_n^+ = \dddot{D_Y} \cap \Phi_n^+ = \dddot{D_Y} \cap \dddot{\Phi}$$ where $\dddot{D_Y} = D_Y \cap H(u_Y)$. Now $\dddot{D}_X$, $\dddot{D}_Y $ and $\dddot{D_e}$ are maximal pointed convex cones of $H(u_Y)$. Therefore $T_Y^{-1}(\dddot{D_e})$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^n$. Now by Theorem \ref{equivalence} There exists an ordered orthonormal basis $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ of $\Bbb{R}^n$ with $$T_Y^{-1}(\dddot{D_e}) = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$ Let $T_1$ be the orthogonal transformation in $O_n$ that sends $e_i$ to $-v_i$, $1 \leq i \leq n$. Then $$T_1^{-1}(T_Y^{-1}(\dddot{\Phi})) = T_1^{-1}(T_Y^{-1}(\dddot{D_e}\cap S^{n })) = T_1^{-1}(T_Y^{-1}(\dddot{D_e}))\cap T_1^{-1}(T_Y^{-1}(S^{n })) = \Phi^+_{n - 1}.$$ Letting $T :H(u_Y) \to \Bbb{R}^n$ denote the isometry $T = T_1^{-1}T_Y^{-1} $, we get $T(\dddot{\Phi}) = \Phi^+_{n - 1}$ and $$ \widetilde{X} = T(\dddot{X}) = T(\dddot{D_X}) \cap T(\dddot{\Phi}) = T(\dddot{D_X}) \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+ \in \mathcal{L}_{n -1}. $$ since $T(\dddot{D_X})$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^n$. Similarly $\widetilde{Y} = T(\dddot{Y}) \in \mathcal{L}_{n -1}$. Using our inductive assumption, we can find $\widetilde{Z} \in \mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$ with $\widetilde{Z} = \widetilde{X}\vee \widetilde{Y}$. Now $\widetilde{Z} = D_{\widetilde{Z}} \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+$ for some maximal pointed convex cone $D_{\widetilde{Z}}$ in $\Bbb{R}^n$ and if $D$ is another maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^n$ for which $ D \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+$ is an upper bound for $\{\widetilde{X}, \widetilde{Y}\}$, then $ D_{\widetilde{Z}} \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+ \subseteq D \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+$. The isometry $T^{-1} : \Bbb{R}^n \to H(u_Y)$ gives a bijection between maximal pointed convex cones in $\Bbb{R}^n$ and maximal pointed convex cones in $H(u_Y)$. Therefore $$\dddot{Z} = T^{-1}(\widetilde{Z}) = T^{-1}(D_{\widetilde{Z}}) \cap T^{-1}(\Phi_{n - 1}^+) = T^{-1}(D_{\widetilde{Z}}) \cap \dddot{\Phi}$$ contains $\dddot{X}$ and $\dddot{Y}$ and if $D_1$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $H(u_Y)$ for which $D_1 \cap \dddot{\Phi}$ contains $\dddot{X}$ and $\dddot{Y}$, then $\dddot{Z} \subseteq D_1 \cap \dddot{\Phi}$. We let $\dddot{D_Z} = T^{-1}(D_{\widetilde{Z}})$, a maximal pointed convex cone in $H(u_Y)$ with $\dddot{D_Z} \cap \dddot{\Phi} = \dddot{Z}$ . Consider $H_{u_Y}^{int} = \{x \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1} | <x, u_Y> < 0 \}$. We have $Y = \dddot{Y} \cup (H_{u_Y}^{int} \cap \Phi_{n}^+$). Now $$X = \dddot{X} \cup \{x \in X | <x, u_Y> < 0\} = \dddot{X} \cup [X \cap (H_{u_Y}^{int} \cap \Phi_{n}^+)]$$ since $\bar{X} \subseteq \bar{Y} \subseteq H_{u_Y}$. Let $D_Z = \dddot{D_{Z}} \cup H_{u_Y}^{int}$. It is clear that $D_Z$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $D_Z \cap H(u_Y) = \dddot{D_Z}$. I claim that $Z = D_Z \cap \Phi^+_n$ is the least upper bound of $\{X, Y\}$ in $\mathcal{L}_n$. Certainly $$X\subseteq \dddot{X} \cup [ H^{int}_{u_Y} \cap \Phi^+_n] \subseteq \dddot{Z} \cup [ H^{int}_{u_Y} \cap \Phi^+_n] \subseteq Z$$ and similarly $Y \subseteq Z$. Now suppose $D'$ is another maximal pointed convex cone of $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with the property that $D' \cap \Phi_n^+$ contains both $X$ and $Y$. We must show that $Z \subseteq D' \cap \Phi_n^+$. We have $\dddot{X} \subseteq X \subseteq D' \cap \Phi_n^+$ and $\dddot{Y} \subseteq Y \subseteq D' \cap \Phi_n^+$. If we let $\dddot{D'} = D' \cap H(u_Y)$, then $\dddot{D'} $ is a maximal pointed cone of $H(u_Y)$ and $\dddot{D'} \cap \dddot{\Phi}$ contains both $\dddot{X}$ and $\dddot{Y}$. Therefore as shown above, $\dddot{Z} = \dddot{D_{Z}} \cap \dddot{\Phi} \subseteq \dddot{D'} \cap \dddot{\Phi} \subseteq D' \cap \Phi_n^+$. Now since $(H_{u_Y}^{int} \cap \Phi_{n}^+) \subseteq Y \subseteq D' \cap \Phi_n^+$, we have that $Z = (\dddot{D_{Z}} \cap\dddot{\Phi}) \cup (H_{u_Y}^{int} \cap \Phi_{n}^+) \subseteq D' \cap \Phi_n^+$. This completes that proof that $Z = X\vee Y$ in $\mathcal{L}_n$.
nodes.section: 5 The least upper bound of two elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on n: transport the traces on H(u_Y) isometrically to L_{n-1} (via Thm 3.12), join there, and glue back the open half space H_{u_Y}^int. A direct check shows the glued cone gives the least upper bound.

assumptions: Let $X, Y \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+$ and $Y = T_Y(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+$.
conclusions: there exists $Z \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with the property that $Z$ is a least upper bound for $\{X, Y\}$.
